Okay, so it's pretty impressive. And again, this was 10 months ago, so AI tutors have only gotten better, I'm sure, in that time. But, I mean, he's not the only one saying this. Four ways AI could revolutionize education technology or how AI is revolutionizing the world of education. cues.zh: 教育领域是不是总用“revolutionize”这个词？这里有一本Sal Khan的书。你在第一个视频里见过他。Brave New Words, How AI Will Revolutionize Education。但我的意思是，他不是唯一这样说的人。AI能彻底变革教育技术的四种方式，或者AI如何变革教育世界。所以很明显，对一场革命的期待就在这里。但事实是，

cues.zh: 期待教育革命的人，至少已经存在100年了。比如Thomas Edison。这是1922年。电影注定会彻底变革我们的教育体系。几年内，它将在很大程度上，甚至完全取代教科书的使用。你还记得100年前我们是怎么摆脱教科书的吧？他说过类似这样的话，

cues.en: The education from a textbook is 2% efficient, whereas education from a motion picture is 98% efficient. I have no idea where he came up with those numbers. I don't think anyone does. But you can imagine that in his time, the motion picture would have seemed like magic. In the same way that first clip I showed you of an AI agent tutoring a kid and doing it somewhat competently, that also seems like magic.
cues.zh: 用教科书接受教育的效率是2%，而用电影接受教育的效率是98%。我完全不知道他从哪得出这些数字。我觉得没人知道。但你可以想象，在他那个年代，电影看起来就像魔法。就像我给你们看的第一段视频里，一个AI智能体辅导孩子，而且做得还算像样，那看起来也像魔法。

cues.en: So you can see why this argument for revolution is kind of convincing. In the 1930s you had people saying radio would revolutionize education.
cues.zh: 所以你能明白，为什么这种革命论调有点说服力。在1930年代，就有人说无线电将彻底变革教育。

cues.en: Why? Because you could get rid of all the teachers, you could just have babysitters in the classroom, and then you'd have the expert radio in, and they could radio in to a thousand classrooms. So immediately you have this economy of scale. And people see the same thing today. Elon Musk says AI education will be like having Einstein as a teacher for every child. The same idea. We're going to scale up the best and the brightest. We're going to have this...
cues.zh: 为什么？因为你可以摆脱所有老师，教室里只要保姆，然后让专家通过无线电接入，他们可以向一千间教室广播。于是立刻就获得了规模经济。人们今天看到的是同样的事。Elon Musk说，AI教育就像给每个孩子都配一个Einstein当老师。同样的想法。我们要把最优秀、最聪明的人规模化。我们将拥有这种……

cues.en: most intelligent entity teaching everyone instead of, I don't know what we have today. Okay, so 1950s, it was TV. Academics actually conducted studies where they would have a lecture going on in one room like this one, then they'd have it videoed and closed circuit TV in the lecture room next door. And they would test the students to see who learned more or less. The answer, no significant difference.
cues.zh: 由最聪明的实体来教导所有人，而不是像现在这样，我也不知道我们现在算什么。好吧，在1950年代，那是电视。学者们真做过研究，他们在一个像这样的教室里讲课，然后录下来，通过闭路电视转播到隔壁的阶梯教室。接着他们去测试学生，看哪边学得多哪边学得少。结果是：没有显著差异。

cues.en: No big surprise, because they're getting basically the same experience, assuming the TV system works reasonably well. Then, in the 1980s, I think people at MIT, anyway, thought that they had it. They thought they had the revolution in education, because the thing we had been missing was interactivity. And now, you could actually interact with the computer, you could go back and forth with it, you could program. So there was this idea that if we taught kids how to program, say, how to program a turtle,
cues.zh: 这并不奇怪，只要电视系统运行良好，他们获得的体验基本上是一样的。到了1980年代，我想至少MIT的人觉得他们找到答案了。他们以为迎来了教育革命，因为我们之前缺少的正是“交互性”。现在，你真的可以和电脑互动了，可以来回交流，还可以编程。所以当时有种想法：如果我们教孩子们编程，比如教他们操控海龟绘图，

cues.en: then they would get better reasoning skills overall. What happened? The kids got proficient at programming the turtle, but those skills did not transfer to other sorts of reasoning. We didn't get better thinkers, and that was the concept. That was why computers and interactive computers and doing this whole turtle programming was meant to revolutionize education once more.
cues.zh: 他们整体的推理能力就会提升。结果呢？孩子们操控海龟编程确实很熟练了，但这些技能并没有迁移到其他推理能力上。我们并没有培养出更好的思考者，而那原本是核心设想。那就是为什么当年人们认为计算机、交互式计算机以及这一整套海龟编程，能够再次彻底变革教育。

cues.en: In the 1990s, you get this, the use of video discs in classroom instruction is increasing every year and promises to revolutionize what will happen in the classroom of tomorrow. I don't know, many of you here may not know what a video disc is. It was a huge CD-like thing, like a DVD. I used to use these when I was in high school, so, you know, they were there. Did they revolutionize education? No.
cues.zh: 到了1990年代，又出现了这种论调：视盘在课堂教学中的应用逐年增加，并有望彻底变革未来的课堂。我不知道，在座很多人可能都不知道视盘是什么了。它是一种像CD一样的大号圆盘，有点像DVD。我上高中时还用过这玩意儿，所以你看，它们确实存在过。它们变革教育了吗？并没有。

Well, MOOCs revolutionize higher education. At least they're asking a question. Revolution hits the universities. No, it's hit. The phenomenon of MOOCs revolutionizing education in the digital age. The online education revolution drifts off course.

Anyway, I hope you take my point. People are all too excited, all too ready to put the word revolutionize next to education. This is old school, new school, it's the same school. What is going on?

cues.en: We shouldn't be using this word revolutionize. You keep using that word. I do not think it means what you think it means. You know it's a good talk if there's a Princess Bride reference. Okay. So why didn't these revolutions materialize or why didn't they eventuate? You could say educational institutions are just they have a lot of inertia. They're not willing to change. We're all just set in our ways. You could say it was just technological overhype.
cues.zh: 我们不该用 revolutionize 这个词。你一直用这个词。我不觉得它的意思是你以为的意思。演讲里要是能引用《公主新娘》，那这演讲就差不了。好。那这些革命为什么没成真，或者说为什么没发生？你可能会说，教育机构就是惯性太大，不愿改变。我们都固守老路。你也可以说，那只是技术炒作过头了。

Five cents. Yes, very good. Now, like I don't think these people are silly. I don't think they're stupid I think they could work it out, you know, if the ball was ten cents and the bat was a dollar more than the ball it would be a dollar ten and so together

Something I love about that clip. So why did they do that? Well...
cues.zh: 它们就会是 1 美元 20 美分，对吧？所以正确答案，显然你们都知道，是 5 美分。那为什么他们都说 10 美分？因为当他们听问题时，这个数字就冒进了脑子里。他们不知道这个数字从哪来，但它就在脑子里，而且听起来很对，于是他们同时脱口而出。真的很神奇，对吧？我很喜欢那段视频的一点。那他们为什么这么做？嗯……

cues.en: The the insights are in this book, which is one of my favorite books of all time thinking fast and slow by Daniel Kahneman So in the book he's talking about our two systems of thought that we've got two things two kinds of processes going on in our brains at one time the fast processes system one and slow processes system two and at the start of one of his chapters he imagines what if there was a Hollywood movie where These systems are turned into characters
cues.zh: 这些洞见就在这本书里，它是我有史以来最喜欢的书之一：Daniel Kahneman 的《思考，快与慢》。在书里，他谈到我们有两套思维系统，我们的大脑里同时有两种过程：快速过程，系统一；慢速过程，系统二。在他某一章的开头，他设想，如果有一部好莱坞电影，把这些系统变成角色，会怎样

cues.en: And so I decided to take that inspiration and run with it. So I created these two characters inside my head. System one is on the left and system two is on the right. Now, system two is kind of the person who you think you are. That's the voice in your head. It's a slow, effortful system.
cues.zh: 于是我就决定接过这个灵感往下做。我在脑子里创造了这两个角色。系统一在左边，系统二在右边。系统二有点像你以为的那个自己。它是你脑中的声音。它是一个缓慢、费力的系统。

cues.en: Thinking takes some effort. If you ask him to multiply like 13 times 17, he's going to say, I don't want to do it. But you could force him to do it. And he can go through a series of steps. So that's the thing about system two is it's slow. It's methodical. It can catch mistakes. It can work through processes. It can think about thinking.
cues.zh: 思考是要费点劲的。如果你让他算比如 13 乘 17，他会说，我不想算。但你可以逼他算。他可以一步步走完流程。所以系统二就是这样：它慢，有条理，能发现错误，能走完过程，能反思思考本身。

cues.en: Now, system one, on the other hand, is rapid fire. This guy is doing things fast in the background. You have no idea that he's doing it. He's collecting all the information from your senses. He's pulling out the relevant information, and he is getting rid of everything else because you're just getting bombarded with stimuli. So he's pulling out those key pieces of information that you're going to work with. And he does all of this without you, the system two thinking conscious thing, really being aware that he's doing it.
cues.zh: 而系统一呢，反应极快。这家伙在后台飞速运转，你根本察觉不到他在做事。他从你的感官收集所有信息，提取出相关的，把其余的统统过滤掉，因为你时刻都在遭受海量刺激的轰炸。所以他提取出那些供你使用的关键信息。而他做这一切时，你，也就是具有思考意识的系统二，压根意识不到他的存在。

cues.en: And you noticed also that he was like in a library setting. So he's sort of associated with all of your long-term memory. So he's got all of that, and that's what allows him to work so quickly and so effectively. And when those people said 10 cents to me, he served up the answer 10 cents. And this guy, System 2, was just like, yeah, 10 cents. I'm not going to think about it. I'm not going to check that answer. He could check the answer, but he doesn't want to because he's lazy. And fair enough.
cues.zh: 你还注意到他就像置身于图书馆一样。所以他某种程度上关联着你的所有长期记忆。他掌握着这一切，这也正是他能如此快速高效运转的原因。当那些人对我说是10美分时，他就直接端出了10美分这个答案。而系统二这家伙就直接接受了，“对，10美分，我懒得去想了，我才不核对这个答案呢。”他本来可以核对，但他不想核对，因为他太懒了。也无可厚非。

cues.en: The goal for us should not be always to use system two, but it should be for us to know when we need system two versus when system one will be fine. So the idea is hopefully you want to optimize, allow system one to handle everything that they can handle, and only hand off to system two things that you need to. Now in my travels, I came across these two characters, and something that I thought about later was that they almost embody system one and system two.
cues.zh: 我们的目标不应该是时刻使用系统二，而是要知道什么时候需要系统二，什么时候系统一就足够了。也就是说，理想情况下你要去优化，让系统一去处理所有它能搞定的事，只把必要的事情移交给系统二。在我的旅途中，我遇到了这两个人，我后来琢磨了一下，他们几乎就代表了系统一和系统二。

cues.en: together so the question that I asked them was like How long does it take for the earth to go around the Sun? Okay, so how long does it take for the earth to go around the Sun? And so even though, like, yes, in theory they should know how to read these notes and they should know what a quarter note is and understand the beats, I can tell you, as someone who played French Horn for several years, I didn't really know how to read music for at least a couple years after I started playing. Like...
cues.zh: 就是让他们弹已经熟知的曲子。这样他们就知道节奏应该是什么样。所以，尽管理论上他们应该学会识谱、知道什么是四分音符并理解节拍，但我作为一个吹过好几年法国号的人可以告诉你，在我开始吹号后的头几年里，我其实根本不会识谱。就像……

cues.en: The music told me what fingers to push down because I could have understood the notes. But in terms of rhythms and things like that, really being able to sight read music, I think it took a couple years. So I think this is one of those things where we limit intrinsic cognitive load by getting students to play songs they already know. Another way to limit intrinsic cognitive load is to slow things down. So anyone who's practicing music, for example, like this harpist, who's a friend of mine, she describes her practice like this. You can.
cues.zh: 音乐告诉我该按下哪些手指，因为我能看懂音符。但就节奏之类的来说，真正能视奏音乐，我觉得花了几年。所以我认为，这类做法之一就是：让学生弹他们已经会的曲子，来限制内在认知负荷。限制内在认知负荷的另一种方式，是放慢速度。比如任何练音乐的人——像这位竖琴手，她是我的朋友——她这样描述自己的练习。你可以。

cues.en: practice everything exactly as it is and exactly as it's written, but at just such a speed that you have to think about and know exactly where you are and what your fingers are doing and what it feels like. So she's really talking about using System 2 there, very slowly, deliberately, effortfully, thinking through every little thing that she's doing in those moments. And then once she does that enough times,
cues.zh: 把一切都完全按原样、完全按谱面写的那样来练，但速度要刚好慢到你必须思考，清楚自己弹到哪儿、手指在做什么、感觉是什么样。所以她其实是在说用系统2，非常慢、刻意、费力地，把当下自己做的每件小事都想透。然后等她这样做足够多次，

cues.en: Enough repetitions of this, you get something that looks like this. Yeah, so good, right? Every time I see superhuman performance, the thing that I'm thinking about is how they have used System 2 very slowly and effortfully to build up that structure in long-term memory that allows them to do things that look so amazing and effortless.
cues.zh: 这样重复足够多次，你就会得到看起来像这样的东西。对，很好，对吧？每次我看到超人般的表现，我想到的都是：他们如何用系统2非常缓慢、费力地在长期记忆里建立起那套结构，让他们能做出看起来如此惊艳又毫不费力的事。

cues.en: It's also at this point that I bring up this idea that discovery learning can be dangerous. You know, when I was going through school, I'd say the dominant paradigm in education was something called constructivism. And the basic tenet of constructivism is that students are active constructors of their own knowledge. Something I do not disagree with. It's basically what I'm saying up here, that system two is about being active and effortful in how we engage with material, how we practice.
cues.zh: 也正是在这里，我要提出这个观点：发现学习可能很危险。你知道，我上学那会儿，我会说教育中的主导范式是所谓的建构主义。建构主义的基本原则是，学生是自己知识的主动建构者。这一点我并不反对。这基本上就是我在上面说的：系统2讲的是，我们在接触材料、练习时，要主动且费力。

cues.en: The problem is, I think some people didn't know how to implement teaching for this constructivist paradigm. Their thinking was, if the students need to be active, then telling won't work. But that's not true. I'm telling you stuff right now. But I bet you're still being active and effortful in your brains, which is the place where you need to be active and effortful. So that was the problem with constructivism.
cues.zh: 问题是，我认为有些人不知道如何为这种建构主义范式实施教学。他们的想法是：如果学生需要主动，那讲授就不管用。但事实并非如此。我现在就在给你们讲东西。但我敢打赌，你们的大脑仍然在主动且费力地运转，而大脑正是你需要主动且费力的地方。所以这就是建构主义的问题所在。

cues.en: It led to some classrooms where people really pulled the scaffolding away from students. I would argue too early So it was we want to teach problem-solving. Here's a problem solve it. You don't know how to do that figure it out construct This is just my personal pet peeve. I have some hangups about constructivism But this is this is where I say discovery learning can be dangerous. I can see flip sides of it for example
cues.zh: 它导致一些课堂里，人们真的把脚手架从学生那里撤走了。我会说，撤得太早了。于是就变成：我们想教解决问题。这儿有个问题，解决它。你不知道怎么做？自己弄明白，建构出来。这只是我个人的小毛病。我对建构主义有些心结。但这就是我说发现学习可能危险的地方。比如，我也能看到它的另一面

cues.en: If you go to a new city, and you don't use a GPS, it's really hard to figure out where you have to go. But if you do it, and you use your System 2 to figure out and follow every street and look at all the signs around and read these things, and you're looking really carefully at everything, at the end of that, you'll probably be able to retrace your steps. If you use the GPS, it'll be much easier for you. You're offloading processing from System 2, you're offloading it to the GPS.
cues.zh: 如果你去一个新城市，又不用GPS，会很难弄清自己该去哪儿。但如果你不用GPS，而是用系统2去弄明白，沿着每条街走，看周围所有路标、读这些信息，真的仔细观察一切，最后你大概能原路返回。如果你用GPS，就会容易得多。你是在把处理从系统2卸载出去，卸载给GPS。

cues.en: Can you find your way back? No. You're going to need the GPS to find your way back. I think there has to be some balance in education between the kind of GPS guidance and the internal guidance. Ideally, I would love to see a gradual phasing out of the support to allow the person to figure out the directions on their own. This has been, I think, well backed up in research of things like the worked example effect. And this is even a further idea of sort of
cues.zh: 你能找到回去的路吗？找不到。你得靠 GPS 才能找回去。我认为在教育中，GPS 式的外部引导和内在引导之间必须取得某种平衡。理想情况下，我希望能逐步撤掉这种支持，让学生自己去摸索方向。我认为这在诸如“样例效应”等研究中得到了很好的印证。这其实是进一步的想法，也就是

cues.en: fading out the assistance as you go. But the idea of first giving someone, hey, here's a problem, and here's how you solve it. Here's a problem that is not quite at the end. Here's a problem partially done, and here's one for you to do from start to finish. But it is this idea of, I'm going to reduce your intrinsic cognitive load. I'm not just going to give you this problem at the end and say, figure it out. I'm going to give you this scaffolding, because I know that what your working memory is is very limited.
cues.zh: 随着学习的深入逐渐淡出辅助。但核心思路是，先给学生展示：“看，这是问题，这是解法。这是一个快做完的问题。这是一个做了一半的问题，而这一个要你从头到尾自己做。” 这背后的理念是：我要减轻你的内在认知负荷。我不会直接把最后那个问题丢给你说“自己想去吧”。我会给你搭好脚手架，因为我知道你的工作记忆非常有限。

cues.en: That system, too, has very limited resources, and I'm not going to tax them with you trying to think about all sorts of things at the same time. I'm going to give you this assistance. So to me, this is the scaffolding that helps system one move through and learn new problems. I think, again, this is kind of a problem we have in complex domains like physics, where to the physics professor, everything's perfectly clear, because their system one is so fully developed. But to a student, it's not.
cues.zh: 系统2的资源也非常有限，我不想让你同时思考各种事情而把它拖垮。我会给你这种辅助。所以在我看来，正是这种脚手架帮助了系统1去推进并学习新问题。我认为，这同样是我们在物理等复杂领域常遇到的问题：在物理教授看来一切都显而易见，因为他们的系统1已经高度成熟；但对学生来说并非如此。

cues.en: So this is the expert novice divide. The professor can't see with the student eyes what that problem looks like, right? Only the student can see it that way. Okay, so what else do we need to do in education? We need to repeat that effortful practice until we achieve mastery. Why is mastery so important? Because when you show a skill with mastery, that means it's now a system one
cues.zh: 这就是专家与新手的鸿沟。教授无法用学生的视角来看待那个问题，对吧？只有学生才会那样看。好，那么在教育中我们还需要做什么？我们需要重复那种需要付出努力的练习，直到完全掌握。为什么精通如此重要？因为当你熟练掌握一项技能时，就意味着它已经进入了系统1的

cues.en: domain. For example, for all of us here in the room, our basic time tables, I imagine, are mastered. They're in system one. You don't have to think about it. What's so useful about that? When you come to do other problems which require that information, you're not going to overload system two when you do it, because all that stuff is automatic. So that's the key. That's how we're going to get better and better performances by building up more and more capabilities which are automatic.
cues.zh: 范畴。比如在座的各位，我想基本的乘法口诀大家都已经掌握了。它们都在系统1里，你根本不用去想。这有什么用呢？当你去做其他需要这些信息的问题时，你就不会让系统2超负荷，因为这些东西都是自动完成的。这就是关键所在。我们要获得越来越好的表现，靠的就是积累越来越多自动化运作的能力。

cues.en: If you never get to the level of mastery, then moving on is going to always cause you problems because you're going to be having to use extra areas in your working memory to deal with thinking about that first before you can think about the other thing. Next, we have increased your main load. So how do you get people to engage in really active thinking, extra level active thinking? One thing that was tried, for example, with this problem, okay, so the bat and ball problem is actually from...
cues.zh: 如果你从未达到精通的水平，那么继续往前走总会遇到麻烦，因为你必须占用工作记忆中的额外空间先去想明白那个，然后才能思考别的事情。接下来，我们增加了关联负荷。那么，如何让人们进行真正积极的思考、更高层次的积极思考呢？比如针对这个问题做过的一个尝试——好，这个球拍和球的问题实际上来自……

cues.en: I think it's called the cognitive reflection test. And I think there's actually three questions on this test. The baton ball problem is only one. But this test has been given out to thousands and thousands of people around the world, including incoming students at very elite colleges. And when you give this test, you typically find that about 90% of people get at least one wrong. At least 90% get at least one of the three questions wrong. And they're all kind of like the baton ball problem in a certain way.
cues.zh: 我记得它叫认知反射测试。这个测试其实有三道题，球拍和球问题只是其中一道。但它被发给了全世界成千上万的人，包括一些顶尖大学的新生。做这个测试时，你通常会发现，大约90%的人至少答错一道。至少90%的人三道题里至少错一道。而且它们某种程度上都像球拍和球问题。

cues.en: So then what some researchers tried was, they thought instead of printing out this test in like really clear font on nice white paper, we are going to print it out in like a terrible, very hard to read font, maybe photocopy it a few extra times so it gets really difficult to read, crumble up the paper or something, and then we'll hand it out. And what happens? Well, the error rate drops to 35%.
cues.zh: 于是一些研究者想：与其把测试用清晰字体印在漂亮白纸上，不如用特别糟糕、非常难读的字体印出来，也许再多复印几次，让它真的很难读，把纸揉皱之类的，然后再发下去。结果呢？错误率降到了35%。

cues.en: making the test harder to read made students more likely to answer it correctly. Why? Because they didn't have that easy, like, okay, I can read it, and an answer immediately comes to mind. They didn't have that experience. Instead, what they had was, oh, this is challenging to read, which kicked their System 2 into action, and so it was activated and was able to find the correct answer. So I'm not suggesting this is a good strategy, just, you know, making things more confusing, but I will say...
cues.zh: 把测试弄得难读，反而让学生更可能答对。为什么？因为他们没有那种轻松的感觉——好，我读完了，答案立刻浮现在脑海里。他们没有这种体验。相反，他们感受到的是：这读起来真费劲，这激活了他们的系统2，于是系统2被调动起来，找到了正确答案。所以我不是说这是个好策略，你知道，只是把东西弄得更混乱，但我要说……

cues.en: It can be effective. And I honestly, I feel like I'm seeing advertisers apply this sort of principle sometimes. In the old days of advertising, like the 50s, 60s, I feel like it was all about having a jingle, showing what your product did, why it was better than your competitors, and then having this great jingle that would just get stuck in your head and you'd all remember the name of the brand and why it's better. And then these days,
cues.zh: 它可能有效。说实话，我觉得广告商有时也在用这个原则。在广告的旧时代，比如五六十年代，我觉得一切都在于有一首广告歌，展示你的产品能做什么、为什么比竞品更好，然后配上那首绝妙的广告歌，让你满脑子都是它，记住品牌名和它好在哪里。而到了现在，

cues.en: I think we've got so bombarded by advertising that System One has got great at tuning it out. And so now a new strategy I see some advertisers employ is let's confuse people. This was a billboard that I saw in Sydney near the beach, and I was definitely intrigued. The power of un, unexplained, television, uncost the earth, unpay more, unspend more. It didn't really tell you anything.
cues.zh: 我觉得我们被广告轰炸得太厉害了，系统1已经非常擅长把它们屏蔽掉。所以现在我看到一些广告商采用的新策略是：让人困惑。这是我在悉尼海滩附近看到的一块广告牌，我确实被吸引住了。un 的力量，unexplained（不解释），电视，uncost the earth（不花天价），unpay more（不多付），unspend more（不多花）。它其实什么也没告诉你。

cues.en: It's like, how is this good advertising? A few days later at a bus stop, I saw this, un-explained. With un, there is no stress, just un-stress. No hassle, just un-hassle. With un, you can undo what you did. You can un-drive through the car wash with a window down. Or un-break dance in front of your teenage son and his mates. Or un-flood the downstairs laundry that now doubles as the pool room. Un makes life relaxing and unreal.
cues.zh: 有 un，就没有压力，只有 un-stress。没有麻烦，只有 un-hassle。有 un，你可以撤销做过的事。你可以开着车窗 un-drive 穿过洗车房。或者在十几岁的儿子和他朋友面前 un-break dance。或者给楼下现在兼作泳池房的洗衣房 un-flood。un 让生活轻松又虚幻。

cues.en: on your life. Be happy and live for now. Don't worry, unworry. What is this an ad for? Insurance. Yes, this is an insurance ad. But how lame are insurance ads? And this is pretty great. So they really got me. So what role is AI going to play if you believe in this picture of education that I've painted? I think the positive role that I see for AI is that it can provide timely feedback.
cues.zh: 掌控你的人生。活在当下，开心就好。别担心，放宽心。这是什么广告？保险。是的，这是一则保险广告。但通常保险广告有多无聊啊？而这个真的很棒。所以它确实打动了我。那么，如果你认同我描绘的这幅教育图景，AI又将扮演什么角色呢？我认为AI能发挥的积极作用，就是它能够提供及时的反馈。

cues.en: And that's essential. When you are learning any skill, you're going to go through the repeated rounds of practice and you're going to need immediate feedback in order to learn. When you're playing the harp, if you miss a note, you know immediately. That's great immediate feedback. If you're practicing tennis and your shot's in or out, you probably know, you know, if it hits the net or goes over, you know right away. So these are really helpful in terms of training your brain. There's some different...
cues.zh: 这一点至关重要。学习任何技能时，你都得经历反复的练习，而且必须获得即时反馈才能学会。弹竖琴时，弹错一个音你立马就知道。这就是绝佳的即时反馈。练习网球时，球是界内还是出界，或者有没有挂网、过网，你立刻就会清楚。所以在训练大脑方面，这些都极其有帮助。但也存在一些……

cues.en: industries and some different professions where people seem like experts, but they're actually not. Stock pickers is one example because you may get some feedback that like maybe this was a good decision or a bad decision. But honestly, the stock market is, at least in the short term, incredibly random. And so that feedback is never very informative for what you should do the next time. This has also been shown with political pundits and some economists, anyone who's looking to predict
cues.zh: 不同的行业和职业，有些人看似专家，实则不然。选股人就是一个例子，因为你可能会得到某种反馈，比如这决定是对还是错。但坦白讲，股市——至少在短期内——是极度随机的。因此这种反馈对于你下次该怎么做，从来都提供不了多少有效信息。在政治评论员和某些经济学家身上也是如此，任何试图去预测……

cues.en: these future trends which are much less reliable in terms of the validity of the environment. So one thing I see AI doing is providing this timely feedback which will really help as we saw in the first case with Saul Kahn and his son. But the thing that I'm really worried about is how AI has this opportunity to reduce effortful practice. I have four kids who are eight, six, four, and zero.
cues.zh: 这些未来趋势的人都一样，其所处环境的有效性要低得多。所以我认为AI能做的一件事就是提供及时的反馈，正如我们在Sal Khan和他儿子的第一个案例中看到的那样，这真的很有帮助。但我真正担心的是，AI有可能减少人们刻意付出的努力练习。我有四个孩子，分别是八岁、六岁、四岁和不到一岁。

cues.en: And I worry about them that if they're going to be, will they write an essay? Will they write 100 essays? If there is a generative AI that can write for them, what forces them to practice crafting those sentences? And if they don't craft those sentences, what happens to their brains? The argument here is that you get good at your command of the English language. You get good at being able to speak in front of people.
cues.zh: 我担心的是，他们未来还会写文章吗？会写上一百篇吗？如果有生成式AI能替他们代写，还有什么能促使他们去练习打磨那些句子？而如果他们不去打磨句子，他们的大脑又会变成什么样？这里的核心观点是，你想要熟练掌握英语，想要擅长当众演讲……

cues.en: at being able to express your thoughts in writing by doing it again and again and again and again and you should suck at the beginning. And you shouldn't let that stop you and you should keep going and going and making slight tweaks and improving and getting feedback and getting going. If they never do that, I really worry. What gets into system one? What is that? Do they have an amazing network of connected knowledge that they can draw on? Do they have things that are automated?
cues.zh: 想要能用文字自如表达想法，全靠一次又一次、周而复始地练习，而且一开始写得很烂也没关系。你不能因此而停下脚步，必须坚持下去，做微调、去改进、获取反馈，然后继续前进。如果他们从来不这样做，我真的很担心。那什么能进入系统一（直觉系统）呢？那又算什么？他们能拥有一个庞大的、可供调用的关联知识网络吗？他们的大脑能够自动化处理这些事情吗？

cues.en: I fear that they won't. How do we force people to have to do that painful, effortful work when there's a magic machine that'll do it for you? That's a big concern. What about drawing? You know, if you can just ask it to make a picture of whatever you like. The bat in the ball was AI, by the way. I can't draw. But again, like, what will happen to people's artistic abilities? So this is, I think, my biggest concern is if it prevents us from going through this
cues.zh: 我很担心大家不会再学了。既然有个神奇的机器能替你搞定，我们又怎么去逼人做那些既痛苦又费力的事情呢？这是个大问题。那画画呢？你想画什么，直接吩咐它一声就行了。顺便提一句，刚才那张球棒和球的图就是 AI 画的。我自己可不会画画。但这又带来了同样的问题：人类的艺术能力会变成什么样？所以我觉得，我最大的担忧就在于，如果它让我们不再经历这种

cues.en: painful, effortful process, which is the core process of learning, using your limited system to resources to engage with things and practice again and again and again, even when it's hard, even when it doesn't feel good, even when you're not great at it. That is my big concern. I wanna come back to these two big questions. Why aren't people learning and why haven't the education revolutions materialized? To the first question, I wanna be a little bit more generous to the people we saw at the beginning.
cues.zh: 痛苦而费力的过程，而这恰恰是学习的核心过程——动用你有限的系统资源去钻研事物，一遍又一遍、反反复复地练习，哪怕很艰难，哪怕感受并不好受，哪怕你一开始并不擅长。这正是我最担心的地方。我想回过头来聊聊那两个核心问题：为什么大家不去学习？为什么那些教育革命始终没有成真？针对第一个问题，我想对演讲开头提到的那些人

cues.en: of this talk. cues.zh: 我是觉得，AI的一大作用就是那种反复操练式的训练，切实让学生多加练习，针对他们正在做的事情给出即时反馈。我认为这可以有一些很强大的用例。不过，真正有风险的用例，是大家直接用它来代劳，而不幸的是，我认为这正是它目前最常用的场景。所以这才是令人担忧的。对，那正是我们必须摒弃的用法。谢谢。好的，请观众提最后一个问题。

cues.en: Thank you for your wonderful talk.
cues.zh: 感谢你精彩的演讲。

cues.en: My question was hinted at prior, and I'd just like to make it a little bit more precise. So I'm a grader for this quantum mechanics course, and I graded my students' midterms recently, and the performance was extremely poor. It was abysmal. And this, in no way, was indicated by their performance on assignments. And of course, I think it's very reasonable to conjecture that this is due to the advent of JET GPT. Students can just copy.
cues.zh: 我的问题前面有人稍微提及过，我想问得更具体一点。我是这门量子力学课程的助教，最近刚批改了学生的期中考试，成绩极其糟糕。简直惨不忍睹。而这在平时的作业成绩中完全看不出来。当然，我觉得完全有理由推测，这是因为 ChatGPT 的出现。学生可以直接抄，

cues.en: the solutions from chat GPT, right, on the midterm they don't have that access. And I think it's very reasonable to argue, oh, perhaps we should change the evaluation methods for classes to be more exam-heavy, less assignment-heavy, but at the same time you can argue that exams aren't the best methods of evaluation either due to performance anxiety and all these other things. So I'm wondering, what do you think is a...
cues.zh: 直接从 ChatGPT 抄答案，对吧，但在期中考试时他们没法用。我觉得有人主张“也许我们应该改变课程的评估方式，多看考试、少看作业”，这很合情合理；但与此同时，你也可以反驳说，考虑到考试焦虑等各种因素，考试也不是最好的评估方式。所以我想知道，你认为什么样的……

cues.en: like a preferred rubric or evaluation method for courses nowadays with the advent of AI. Yeah. I mean, the first thing that came to mind is maybe the way that assignments are done now shouldn't be the way they're done in future. Like maybe assignments need to be done in the same way that midterms are done to remove that risk. Because I really worry that that is how you build...
cues.zh: 比如随着 AI 的到来，现在课程更倾向采用哪种评分标准或评估方法。是的。我的意思是，我首先想到的是，也许现在的作业布置方式在未来不该再沿用了。比如作业也许得像期中考试那样去完成，以此规避那种风险。因为我真的很担心，这种方式正是你构建……

cues.en: that long term, that huge structure, that's what we're after. And if we're not building that, then yeah, by the time you get to a midterm or the final, it's too late. The practice has to come in the lesson. I can tell you that when I was lecturing first year physics at UTS, the University of Technology in Sydney,
cues.zh: 那种长期、宏大的认知结构的方式，而这正是我们的目标。如果我们不这么做，那么到了期中或期末考试，一切就都太晚了。练习必须贯穿在平时的课堂中。我可以告诉你，当年我在悉尼科技大学（UTS）教大一物理时，

cues.en: I had like stacks of cards at the front of my lecture that said in huge letters A and B on one and C and D on the other. And I would force the students to come and get these cards at the beginning of every lecture. It was a 400 seat lecture theater. And then as I would go through, I would ask a question maybe once a minute or once every two minutes and they'd have to hold up these cards. And that's really helpful for me as a lecturer to make sure that
cues.zh: 讲台前面放着成叠的卡片，上面印着大大的字母，一张写着 A 和 B，另一张写着 C 和 D。每堂课一开始，我都会要求学生上来拿这些卡片。那是一个能容纳 400 人的阶梯教室。讲课过程中，我大概每隔一两分钟就会提一个问题，他们必须举起这些卡片。作为讲师，这对我非常有帮助，能确保

cues.en: they are where I think they are. It's also really helpful for them in that it keeps system two engaged. It keeps them having to make that decision every few minutes, which stops them from, for example, falling asleep, which deactivates both system one and two. But it's also really easy to tune out. And then that's also not helping. So the whole point of getting this back and forth, even in a large lecture theater just with these cards, I mean, was my attempt at
cues.zh: 他们的进度跟我想象的一致。这对他们自己也大有裨益，因为这能调动他们的系统二思维。这迫使他们每隔几分钟就得做一次判断，能防止他们打瞌睡，打瞌睡会让系统一和系统二都停摆。但即便不睡，也很容易走神，那同样无济于事。所以即便在阶梯大教室里，仅仅依靠这些卡片进行互动，也就是为了

cues.en: making this interaction and getting people to be thinking all the time being really mentally active. So I'd say we have to do the same thing with this work that they're doing, with the assignments. It has to be done. We've got to find some way to make an isolation booth or something.
cues.zh: 创造这种交流，让大家时刻都在思考，保持高度的大脑活跃。因此我认为，对他们平时做的作业，我们也必须采取同样的方法。必须得这样做。我们得想办法弄一个隔间考核之类的环境。

cues.en: Can I just say one more thing? So I think though when you get into higher education, especially in physics, the higher up you are, the longer it takes to complete a question. For instance, on a three-hour exam, there are probably only like three questions because it takes an hour to do each. And so reconciling that in a university setting is much more difficult because you can't just complete a question within the spend of a few minutes and then give an answer, right? So could you comment?
cues.zh: 我能再补充一句吗？不过我觉得进入高等教育阶段，特别是在物理学领域，年级越高，完成一道题所需的时间就越长。例如在三个小时的考试中，可能一共就只有三道题，因为每道题都得花上一个小时。所以在大学环境下去平衡这一点要困难得多，因为你不可能在短短几分钟内就做完一道题并给出答案，对吧？对此你怎么看？

cues.en: No, I mean, it's a really good point. I just don't see any way of getting away from the idea of there's going to have to be assessments at some point. And I know that sucks from like a structural and logistic perspective. But like, there's no other way. If you're not learning the material, you're not graduating. Just the way it is. I thought that I was an amazing lecturer for my time.
cues.zh: 不，我觉得你提得很好。我只是觉得，我们无论如何都避不开这样一个事实：到头来终究得有评估环节。可以是期中和期末考试。如果有人因为平时不好好做作业而挂科，那也只能去接受这个现实。我知道从体制和实操角度来看这很残酷，但确实别无他法。学不会这些知识，就拿不到学位，现实就是这么残酷。想当年我还觉得自己是个极优秀的讲师呢。
